title: Is it even arguable that the sound design of pre 2000-ish was vastly superior?

commenti.body:
I see what you're saying and I agree in some respects but when it comes to sound design I tend to prefer the modern trend towards naturalistic sound you barely notice rather than an emphasized sound design. While there's a lot of great full and rich sound design in a lot of old movies, there's just as many scenes where I'll see someone walking on carpet and theres still a distinct clacking footstep that sounds and feels unnatural to me, like they were more focused on representing an action through sound than actually thinking through what that would sound like to an observer. 

 In general, I think the trend for filmmaking the past 20 years or so has been towards "invisible filmmaking" where many elements of film have aspired to be so smooth and natural that you don't even notice it unless you're looking out for it. You might even forget you're watching a carefully crafted production. The opposite of New Wave ideals in some ways. Editing in particular has aimed to be as smooth of a flow as possible in most productions, but cinematography and sound design have been similarly affected. I'm more against invisible filmmaking when it comes to visuals that sound, but opinions can vary.

I generally agree, with the exception of cinematography, where I find modern trends to be anything but invisible. We get all sorts of fake handheld effects, swerves between speakers rather than cuts, zooms that intentionally rubber band. Of course there are worse offenders and exceptions, but I look forward to the day when smooth and truly invisible camera work returns.

You’re right that there are some overemphasized sounds that some times don’t make sense, but I’ll gladly take that bad with all of the good.

Frankly, I’m just glad someone else has noticed. Obviously, I strongly disagree with you. But at least my thesis has been somewhat validated.

To add to your point, have you listened to the pendulum-swing of the chains near the sluices in Tarkovsky's *Stalker* or the splashing of feet through water in *Mirror* lately? I love Tarkovsky, but these just aren't very convincing. He's a master, but Soviet special effects from before 1980 leave something to be desired (I might also refer to his attempts at rain which rather obviously leaves the characters further away entirely dry in *Andrei Rublev*).

60’s and 70’s sound design was its peak for me. The isolationism and amplification in the mixing has a peak-shift appeal to the brain that modern cinema doesn’t achieve. And the static you mentioned really works to build anticipation and even connects visual cuts to feel smoother.

I completely agree that it’s better and it goes beyond just nurtured taste.

Nothing like those old **CLACKING** shoes on a silent street…
Spot on.

I know exactly what you mean, but I don't think contemporary is any worse necessarily.

Sometimes that every cig, every footstep, every single action has its designated sound...isn't wonderful.

"Pre-2000-ish" covers a lot of ground.

The sound design in movies in the 1960s and '70s is uneven at best and sometimes awful, even in otherwise well-made movies. Harsh, shrill, limited library of stock sounds. My ears bleed whenever glass breaks in a '70s movie.

Technology and technique improved a lot in the '80s and '90s.

I don't think it's so much sound design but dialogue mixing. 

I think some directors just don't pay enough attention to the importance of having audiences hear the spoken dialogue.

The IMAX version of the opening sequence in The Dark Knight Rises as shown in' mission impossible four' had Bane talking with a bit of a deeper inflection but the audience is viewing this prologue didn't understand it and..

 I think Warner Bros is a studio put its foot down and had Tom Hardy ADR an extensive amount of his lines as Bane.. 

And I think that was a wise decision. 

I think parts of Dunkirk have lines that are hard to hear, and entire chunks of Tenet have characters talking in a way that's really hard to discern - - my theory is that since the latter entries aren't part of a franchise, they gave Nolan a longer leash for post production, which could include ADR, but Nolan has gone on record saying he doesn't use ADR to redo line takes ( I think there's an article on Indiewire with this interview) 

As for sound effects, as long as it's not the Wilhelm scream in a dramatic scene I'm not too picky. 

I do like hearing the holler of a TIE fighter zooming by or the shwiiing of a sword being unsheaved, but unless the sound effect is distractingly cheesy like a slide whistle, it doesn't distract from the immersiveness of the film.

My mind immediately went to The Killing of a Chinese Bookie, which had a lot of glaring sound issues and an overall low quality audio track which actively hindered my enjoyment of the overall film. 

It's not a problem for every older film, but I do appreciate the standard of unobtrusive sound design that's been established in recent decades.

I have an abiding love the sound of footsteps in films from the seventies.

I know there's some modern musicians like Jack White who deliberately try and record with analogue methods because they love the sound. And there are modern directors like Tarantino who shoot on analogue film. But are there any modern directors who record the sound on tape on a Nagra and mix it on tape to try and get that old, classic sound?

It really is subjective. Your post makes me think of the hard sound cuts in The Exorcist. The use of contrast in the sound track of that film adds to the feeling of unsettledness.

I feel like contemporary films are less literal than the films of the late 20th century, and I think younger audiences respond to a more naturalistic use of sound. The decrease in theatricality is perceived by younger audiences as more relatable, as opposed to the overall obviously artificial approaches of the past. 

I don't personally subscribe to this but I can see how younger audiences perceive media differently. They have grown up with media with far more sophisticated production techniques.

Furor over *Tenet* aside, this is not something I've noticed as a rule, and this is coming from someone whose favorite era of filmmaking was the 1970s. I think sound design is often incredible today—take last year's *Zone of Interest*, for example. If comparing sound design in, say, the 1990s to the 2020s, I could only judge that on a film-by-film basis. In recent years, I remember films like *Memoria*, *Drive My Car*, *Pacifiction*, and *The Northman* as being sonically compelling.

I think i know what you mean. Old films can have terrible sound of course, but if done well, there is a sense of being in the room with the actors - rather than every single track and microsecond being  fine-tuned for maximum extreme cool factor. Things can start to feel nu-natural past a point. There are still films that do what you like... they're just lower budget films.

I don't know about that. i think it is definitely arguable. the sound design of mad max fury road, or dunkirk or The Batman or recently Alien Romulus is just stupendous. I don't think the sound design feats of some of these movies can be compared to.

I'm just here to say Zodiac was awesome for this. And Caché. REC. No Country For Old Men. Blue Ruin. And since, I got to watch it recently, In A Violent Nature was too.

I think it depends more on what you're watching. Because something with a massive score behind it isn't going to hit as hard as movies where there isn't as much non-diegetic sound. At least if that's what you're looking for.

That sound you hear is millions of *Portrait of a Lady on Fire* fans screaming in outrage.

Seriously though, I love that movie's sound design. Almost all diegetic sound. Footsteps on wood, waves crashing on the beach, charcoal scratching on canvas, crackling wood in the fireplace. The occasional line of dialogue.

Your thesis would be stronger with examples to discuss in-depth. Why don't you provide some?
Ever seen McCabe and Mrs Miller? I could barely hear anything. Ugh.
No, but it's been on my list for a little while. I'm disappointed to hear about the bad audio!
It was even spoken about in reviews at the time supposedly. Maybe the new criterion 4k has better sound I dunno.

To that movie's credit, the dialogue is often less important than the vibe if the room, especially in crowded scenes. People mumble, they speak over each other, etc. It gives a lived-in and realistic feeling to the community.
Congrats, you’ve just discovered a Robert Altman film. I know this feeling can be disconcerting and even a little annoying - but I promise you, that’s the intention.
[removed]

I have heard the same squeaky door sound reused in countless "old" movies. And of course there's the famous Wilhelm scream.

Any time I hear something that's clearly foley, it takes me out of the element. Good sound design should be invisible, in my opinion.

Could not disagree more. There was a far lower expectation for sound back then. It's only become more convincing. It's very easy to see all the dialogue they used to dub over, often poorly (looking at you Fellini). That said, I have a fondness for the sound of old movies.

I mostly watch old movies, and one of the amazing things about classic Hollywood is the 100% uniform obsession with clarity and seamless design. And it really was an obsession; you can barely tell there were directors at all in most 30s-50s Hollywood movies because the work was done so invisibly. Back then 'sound design' meant hiding a mic in a flower pot and making sure the floorboards didn't creak (they had carpenters wearing slippers running out between takes). Hollywood is still largely like this.

In the modern Hollywood film, what I hate is the omnipresent goddamned insane compression + digital reverb that gets applied to the mix after the fact, which makes it so you can't hear most things distinctly. It's liberally, even ruthlessly, applied to all the effects- and star-driven films in particular. It's exhausting. Sound compressors, in case anyone doesn't know, automatically regulate and even-out volume; they lift up quiet sounds and lower loud sounds, and kind of prioritize the loudest sounds (like how cheap cameras auto-focus based on movement/lighting). The studios often seem to just slap it on the whole movie mix! When music is playing under the effects and they're all compressed together and doused with reverb it just turns into a big jumble. Basically, IMO, many movies are now too sound-designed and everything is fighting for your attention. It's all super artificial; movies too-often sound like how the photography too-often looks. Everything gets smeared together artificially so that only the loudest, most distinct things break through and register on your perception. If the voice (or whatever) isn't the loudest thing in the mix, it just gets swallowed up and lost in the smear. The standard effects they use for processing do sound amazing/impressive (especially some of the massive reverb effects that cushion the sounds), and I get why they do it, but it rarely serves the movie except to kind of unify it into one continuous soundscape. When people are complaining about Nolan this is what they're really sore about IMO. His superb mixing just gets overwhelmed by the effects and post-processing, his detail-oriented approach is at odds with what the effects then mindlessly do to the mix. I think he's the best guy going for sound design and it's kind of sad he just gets crucified for caring about and applying artistry to it. 

This perceived-by-me trend is really damaging to the music in movies, too. There are astounding scores that you can't tell are any good until you actually buy the record! Like *Solo* for instance, which isolated is 2 hours of amazing super-syncopated musical nirvana, but in the movie it's wallpaper you can scarcely even hear except when the Millennium Falcon theme surfaces out of the murk of sound effects. I found myself watching the movie over and over again (it's not a great movie) and couldn't figure out what the attraction was until I went and got the soundtrack! Now I just listen to that, ha.
I think they did that on purpose
[removed]
[removed]
Im thinking okder Bond movies. Those screaming car tires. Or the gun shots.

I do feel like the fidelity of dialogue has decreased in recent years. I dunno if maybe my hearing is just going but there are plenty of movies where I gotta strain just to understand what's being said. 



That said there have been plenty of recent movies where the sound design blew me away. From smaller things like the 2nd new planet of the apes movie having the sound of rain be so clear and crisp that I almost thought it was raining in the theater. And then you have something more dramatic like Bladerunner 2049's sound design. The scene in the malfunctioning music lounge is just amazing.
[removed]

But but Ive learned that ld shoes do clack more, I had a pair of vintage style work boots made in the USA and those boots are loud, even on concrete or asphalt. They just have a heft to them and an at night walking alone, I get to feel like I am in one of those old movies.

The plastic crap most people wear now is basically silent.
Yeah that's fine, but when you're straining to understand what people are saying, that can be an issue.

That's a broad statement that really doesn't hold up.

There are a lot of variables:
1. technology advancements
2. the talent and artistry of a sound designer
3. the quality of the sound in print (e.g. a cheap DVD release of an old film might have mono audio and may have used a lower quality source, whereas you might be watching criterion remasters of old films)

not sure what post-2000 films you are talking about...big budget franchise IPs certainly tend to have less thoughtfully designed sound. something like Portrait of a Lady on Fire, however...
I've seen many Robert Altman films, this was different, I could understand what people were saying in his other films, this was more of a technical issue than a creative one.

I love the 1990's sound mixes. When Dolby Digital launched and DTS and SDDS entered the market shortly thereafter, they all got into this competition to see who could blow the roofs off the cinemas... and it was GLORIOUS. 

A lot of the Laserdiscs from that era had the theatrical mixes ported directly over - but unfortunately when DVD came along they started doing specific remixes designed for the basic home video user and they started to get "shy" with how bombastic they mixed these home versions. 

As tv's got slim so did the speakers, so these home mixes sound worse and worse. I'll run old Beta and VHS HiFi tapes through Dolby PLII in my home theatre and I'm totally blown away by how loud and full they sound by comparison to many of their DVD/Blu counterparts.
i think call me by your name is another recent example of asmr-like sound design. the way water sloshes in that film makes me want to go swimming

Yeah I always thought that was the point? Like when they're in that noisy bar, it's really difficult to hear the dialogue but it felt like he wanted you to struggle to overhear the conversation as though you, too, were in the bar trying to eavesdrop, essentially.

Did I turn the subtitles on? Yes. But the ambient talking was *so* loud that I figured it had to be intentional.

I’ve been thinking about this for years but I watched Manhunter and Videodrome over the last 2 days and both have unreal sound designs. Manhunter also has 2 scenes where songs play in whole, which is something that doesn’t happen much at all anymore that’s awesome.
Thanks for examples. I don't recall Videodrome's sound as anything special. Anyway, I think your thesis is too vague to agree or disagree with. I don't know what an "average" movie is.

Time and time again, when you ask musicians where they listen to their albums during the mixing process, they almost always say "in the car".

The car is where most people are going to hear a piece of music and if it sounds good there, it'll sound good anywhere.

For movies, most people are watching at home, so directors need to have a living room setup where they watch (and listen) to their movies on a basic, normal setup.

Nolan and other directors need to take the example of musicians and take the time to figure out how the experience plays to a normal person.

It ain't hard to do.

I can tell you what I THINK the difference is - 

TLDR: it's those meddlin' video game sound editors. Sounds rick-dickulous but it is kinda true.

So here's the story - I have an award winning short and was in the final stages of cleaning up the sound design. Friend of the Sound Designer wanted to mix the sound - came highly recommended. When we got the final back, all the tones, dialogue, and sound f/x were all blended together. They were THERE, but they all kind of *whooshed* by without landing on any solid notes - it all just blended together. 

My partner and I took the project to our trusted audio post house and sound designer - he told us he's seen this a LOT. That it originates from - I kid you not - video game sound design. They build this constant WALL of sound rather than hitting marks and delineating and celebrating moments, including the audio. 

So - there is that.

Another item I have noticed - oftentimes in films today, there is no room tone mixed into the scenes. I attribute this to not shooting on locations and instead on sound stages and v/fx labs/green screens.

Mix these things together and you have - what I can hear - is todays filmic audio style.

I think there's more emphasis on realism these days, where as older movies were more about being dramatic and entertaining. Personally I do tend to prefer the older style of filmmaking, and modern auteurs who harken back to older styles.

I think you’re over complicating things for yourself. Pick a random film from the last 10 years and a random film from like..I don’t know, 68? There will be a very noticeable difference in the sound. You will hear every footstep taken in film in 68. Everything a character does will most likely have a very pronounced sound attached to it.
I wonder if that’ll turn into another coconut effect; used as a sound we’re familiar with even when not logical to the context.

Random with what distribution? Uniformly random picks are likely to end up on garbage that nobody watches. If we focus on, say, the ten highest grossing films from 1968 and from 2023, you may well have a point (I haven't seen a majority of them). But "random" and "average" are too nebulous.

It's definitely not less produced now, it's a LOT more work, more teams of workers, more complex layers, etc.

I agree there's a certain charm to 'warm' vintage sounds, in everything, but it's not 'better sound design'.

There's also a huge amount of different projects across the world that do all kinds of styles of sound post production. Maybe you mean Hollywood specifically? And even then, the blockbusters. Indie movies have a lot of variance. 

I am a sound mixer and designer. I am not saying there wasn't a lot of good sound design back then, yes, I quite enjoy some, but certainly a lot less produce, more crude and simple, and a lot of bad mixing moments, harsh sounds, repeating same libraries, noticeable adr, etc. None of that is good, you're just used to it. Stylistically, anything is possible now in sound and you're only limited by your creativity.

I mean Nolan is infamous for loud fucking mixes and bumbling dialogue. Not really a reflection of modern cinema as a whole, he's specifically the single biggest advocate of loud shit, neverending music and unintelligible dialogue.

There's hardly any pro sound designers in film that came from/learned from video games. If it happens it is statistically insignificant, and it is often the other way around, film sound designers moving over to the growing game industry. I disagree that as an overall reason.

As for room tones, at least I've always learned to have room tones in every interior scene as one layer of ambiences, you don't necessarily record them in set anymore as there's a billion sound libraries and directors don't wanna waste time making everyone silent for recording those on set.

What has impacted and reduced room tone noise is that dialogue cleaning tools are much better now. So we take away noise from dialogue, and those room tones just feel like noise and vast majority of directors ask for the noise to be reduced once they hear how clear and clean and forward the dialogue sounds (when properly recorded and cleaned). 

Very few choose to use the more raw dialogue with noisy room tones, and I believe if we time traveled to the 70s and brought them the tools we have now, directors then would make the same choice.
Scorsese’s movies have that where you feel like you’re in the room with the characters, but obviously he’s a “old film” director. Nice to see he’s kept that feel though over the years.

> There's hardly any pro sound designers in film that came from/learned from video games.

Valid point. 

I'd propose it's more an element of standardization. Movies are geared toward teens and teens play videogames. They key into that style of sound design and so sound design might be going in that direction.

As for my experiences - with indie and micro budget, if you can get any experienced sound designer (or DP, etc.) you might likely jump at the chance.

As for the tools - I often wonder what kind of amazing audio mixes the great Robert Altman might have created today.
I think his team hadn’t fully ironed out the technical process on that one yet. Still one of my all time favorites though.

I appreciate your input. You’re obviously far more knowledgeable on the topic.

What are the movies that made you want to be a sound designer?
Also, there's so much bass in a lot of modern sound mixes. Someone's talking on the screen and it's booming around the whole theatre. It sounds so stupid.
[removed]

Watching the FX TV show *Groteskuerie* and the lack of room-tone combined with the clinical MOS dialogue makes it feel sterile and wildly off-putting. The whole thing feels like something an AI put together. There's no human touchstones to it at all.

I think sound design became more interesting once digital audio mixing became the norm, which I believe was somewhere in the 90s. Before then, soundscapes seemed 'simple', for lack of a better expression. Once digital mixing and editing became more commonplace, sound designers could express more control and add more depth to the mixes.

However, I also grew up in the 90s, and so I have a lot of nostalgia for that era, and 80s movies sound far less fully developed to my ear.

If you're just referring to creative uses of sound in storytelling and immersion, that might be more down to directors less conscious use of sound and focusing too much on the images. The push to just shoot coverage in production and fixing it in post may also bee a culprit here, because sound often needs to be supported by deliberate camera placement. You can't insert a richly textured shot of a match being stuck if you don't have a closeup of the match that also relishes in the details of the surfaces involved.

But I'm sure there's also selection bias here. We forgot all the bad movies that had generic/boring sound design from the older decades, so we can only think of the good ones, and then comparing that against all current movies, good and bad.

> Harsh, shrill, limited library of stock sounds.

I can hear that cartoon lightning sound effect in my head as I read this lmao

Absolutely it's interesting how early radio shows where the sound effects team was vital, played a role in this


It seems when radio stopped being that way films also started to gradually change becoming less auditory


So I think partly it's a product of these wonderful new mediums where simply hearing a familiar sound was exciting


Then that paradigm morphs into new sensations


It's like mmorpgs in the early 2000s, we'd all just wander around doing mundane tasks inefficiently and it felt so damn cool
[removed]

That's not even getting into issues like the old spaghetti westerns where they re-recorded the dialog in a sound booth in a different language from what the actors were even speaking on screen, so there is obviously not even a chance to get the lip sync correct.

One of the things that brings me out of a scene most quickly -- and this will still happen sometimes today -- is when you have dialogue that was obviously recorded in a sound booth for a scene where the actors are outdoors or in some other kind of large space.  Otherwise, for the most part these days, I'm sure a lot of dialogue is re-recorded and I don't even know it, because they are good at adjusting it to sound like it was recorded in the appropriate-sized space.

Doesn't this depend a lot on genre these days?  I would tend to agree that for action films we see a lot of what you're describing, but for most drama, off hand I would tend to say it is more natural/invisible.

The only thing I generally object to about sound mixes these days is that I feel like the dynamic range is often more than I find comfortable.  Nolan is obviously an extreme case for this, where people feel like the dialog level is too low, but ultimately I think it's more often the case that people don't want to tolerate the ear-splitting levels of the loud effects if you were to put the dialog at a level that is easy to hear -- even with a good center channel speaker.

But you aren't going to have that on an old movie from the '70s.  Even something like the original Star Wars with a lot of sci-fi effects in it, explosions, etc., those effects aren't trying to be realistically loud, so you can set the volume where the dialog is easy to hear and you also won't feel like you'll need a hearing aid tomorrow after the death star explodes.

Even then, I can see the argument that the modern approach is more realistic, but in the extremes, realistic isn't always better.

For difficulty hearing dialogue, I usually put it down more to the loud effects being too loud for my taste/comfort.  Even with a good center channel, I do have issue with dialog at times and I think the main thing is just that I don't want to turn it up so loud to hear the dialog because I feel like I'm losing my hearing when there are explosions or gun fire or whatever.

This doesn’t bother me much, but what does is constant music.  It’s not even solely a modern trend.  I’ve seen many action sequences in particular that I thought would have benefited from silence in the music so we can absorb the visceral sounds of the action.   It’s fatiguing when there’s constant music.

Remember the pod race from the phantom menace?  It always stuck out to me that in a Star Wars film the first half of an action sequence is totally music free,  you can take in all the fantastic F1 inspired sound design,  then the music drops in near the finale and it has greater impact.
Did you see Anatomy of a Fall? There were zooms were I thought: Don’t do that, even if you want to say something with it!
[removed]

I liked being able to clearly hear dialog in the before time. I assumed it was hearing loss, I let it be a thing I was sad about. Then I watched some old TV/movies and realized no it's the sound design. Now it makes me different sad.
